old: Removing H+ from HCO3− leaves CO32−: the same C and three O atoms, no H, and a 2− charge (two O atoms carry −1). H2CO3 is the conjugate acid, CO2 has lost an O and an OH, and formate (HCO2−) has lost an O atom rather than an H+.
new: Removing H+ from HCO3− leaves CO32−: the same C and three O atoms, no H, and a 2− charge (two O atoms carry −1). H2CO3 is the conjugate acid, CO2 has lost a whole OH− (an O, the H and the charge), and formate (HCO2−) has lost an O atom rather than an H+.
why: HCO3- (1 H, 3 O) minus CO2 (0 H, 2 O) = OH-; 'an O and an OH' would remove two O atoms

old: This structure has lost an O atom and a charge as well. A conjugate pair differs by one H⁺ only.

why: CO2 = HCO3- minus OH-; the original omits that the H is gone too

old: A six-membered ring (thiane) needs five CH<sub>2</sub> groups between the two C–Br carbons plus S; 1,4-dibromobutane has only four carbons, so the ring formed has one S and four C.
new: A six-membered ring (thiane) needs a five-carbon chain (1,5-dibromopentane) plus S; 1,4-dibromobutane has only four carbons, so the ring formed has one S and four C.
why: Thiane = S + 5 CH2; a 1,5-dibromide has three CH2 between the two C–Br carbons, not five
